tip: Τα μετρητά (ta metritá) = cash – normally used in the plural in Greek.
Μεγαλύτερη (meghalíteri = bigger) is the comparison form of μεγάλος (meghálos = big); it takes -ύτερη, not the usual -ότερη.
Greek has no to-form of the verb: I want to try becomes θέλω να δοκιμάσω (thélo na dhokimáso), literally I want that I try.
Η ουρά (i urá) = the queue – literally the tail.
Πριν goes straight onto the verb with no να (na): πριν φύγω (prin fígho) = before I leave.
Στον χασάπη (ston khasápi) = at the butcher's; χασάπης is the everyday word, while κρεοπωλείο (kreopolío) is the formal word on the shop sign.
Σε δέκα λεπτά (se dhéka leptá) = in ten minutes – here λεπτά means minutes, not cents.
The ending -πωλείο (-polío) marks a shop that sells: άνθος (ánthos = flower) gives ανθοπωλείο (anthopolío = flower shop), so shop signs start to decode themselves.
Η γιορτή (i yortí) = name day – in Greece it is often celebrated as much as a birthday.
Φέρνει (férni = brings) does the delivery work: φέρνει τα ψώνια στο σπίτι (férni ta psónia sto spíti) = they bring the shopping home, meaning they deliver.
Έβρεχε (évrekhe) = it was raining – the past form for weather that went on, not a single finished event.
Εννιά με πέντε (eniá me pénde) = nine to five – με links the two times where English uses to.
Ο/η συνάδελφος (o/i sinádhelfos) = colleague – the same word for a man or a woman; only the article changes.
Πριν από goes in front of a noun: πριν από το μεσημεριανό (prin apó to mesimerianó) = before lunch.
Το ρεπό (to repó) = a day off work – a French loanword that keeps the same form in every position.
Το αφεντικό (to afendikó) = the boss – it takes the neuter article το, even though it means a person.
Σχολάω (skholáo) = I finish work or school – τι ώρα σχολάς; (ti óra skholás) is the everyday way to ask.
Ο φραπές (o frapés) = iced instant coffee, here in the object form φραπέ (frapé) – a Greek office classic since the sixties.
Coffee names are normally masculine, so you order with έναν, not ένα: έναν φρέντο (énan frédo), έναν μέτριο (énan métrio).
The ending -άκι (-áki) is often warmth rather than size: καφεδάκι (kafedháki) = a nice little coffee, from καφές (kafés).
The ending -ονται (-onde) carries the get-done-to sense on its own: κουράζονται (kurázonde = they get tired), with no extra word for get or become.
Έπεσε η γραμμή (épese i ghramí) = the line dropped – the usual way to say a call cut out.
Οι διακοπές (i dhiakopés) = a holiday or vacation – normally used in the plural.
Η κίνηση (i kínisi) = traffic, literally movement – έχει κίνηση (ékhi kínisi) = there's traffic.
Θέλει (théli = wants) also does duty for takes with a stretch of time: θέλει σαράντα λεπτά (théli saránda leptá) = it takes forty minutes.
Βιάζομαι (viázome) = I'm in a hurry – Greek uses one verb where English uses be plus an adjective.
Προλαβαίνω (prolavéno) = I have time for, or I catch in time – δεν προλαβαίνω (dhen prolavéno) = I can't manage it.
Spoken Greek often drops στο before a place like this: πάω γυμναστήριο (páo yimnastírio) = I go to the gym.
Ο μισθός μπαίνει (o misthós béni) = the salary goes in – that is how Greeks say it lands in the account on payday.
Με πήραν τηλέφωνο (me píran tiléfono) = they phoned me – Greek takes a phone rather than making a call.
